--- Meeting Header ---
Date: 2026-04-14
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 46 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Liam Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Maya Ortiz (Galaxy Head of Product), Derek Sloan (Galaxy CTO), Aisha Khan (Platform Engineer)

--- Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be fuzzy) ---
Redwood demo of hosted API for chat/text gen. Covered streaming responses, key request params (temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop), retry logic and idempotency tokens, and brief tour of Console + Optimize. Customer asked about latency, cost tradeoffs, VPC and KMS. Agreed to follow-ups: pricing and security docs, benchmark script, POC scoping.

--- Topics ---
1) Customer context / current stack
2) Hosted API features: streaming, params, retries
3) Console & Optimize brief
4) Security and deployment questions (SSO, KMS, VPC)
5) Next steps / actions

--- Transcript ---
00:00 Liam Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Liam from Redwood, I run partnerships in the Retail vertical. With me is Priya, she's our solution engineer.
00:07 Priya Singh: Hi all, thanks for having us. We'll do a quick run through of the hosted API for chat and text generation basics and then leave time for Q&A.
00:17 Maya Ortiz: Thanks, excited — quick context, we're building in-session personalization for our web checkout and a marketing chat assistant. Low latency matters, but we also wanna keep model costs reasonable.
00:28 Derek Sloan: And on infra side we need to understand if hosted works with our security needs or if we need Dedicated or Private.
00:35 Liam Chen: totally, that's exactly what we usually scope. Quick qual: what's your current traffic profile? peaks, qps?
00:43 Aisha Khan: Right now the prototypes are 10-20 rps but expected to ramp to 200 rps during sales days, typical payloads are short prompts, ~25-60 tokens.
00:55 Priya Singh: good to know. For hosted API the streaming path is optimized for low tail latency — we use a continuous streaming endpoint that begins sending tokens as soon as they're decoded. It's compatible with HTTP/2 and websockets.
01:10 Maya Ortiz: How does streaming interact with retries? if a client disconnects do you re-request and duplicate tokens?
01:18 Priya Singh: good question — we recommend an idempotency token per user request. If you reconnect and supply the same token, Redwood will detect previously completed streams and can return a resume or an indication that the result is already available. Retries for transient errors are safe when you use idempotency, otherwise you might get duplicates.
01:33 Derek Sloan: any weird caveats with partial results and KV cache?
01:38 Priya Singh: the K-V cache we maintain is per session for chat. If you do multiple incremental calls with the same session id the KV cache speeds up subsequent tokens. Partial results streaming doesn't commit to the KV cache until the generation completes — that avoids corrupting state on retries. (transcription: K V cache sometimes shows as K-V cache or K V chache in older docs)
01:55 Liam Chen: on params: temp, top_p, max_tokens — quick primer?
02:01 Priya Singh: sure — temperature controls randomness, top_p is nucleus sampling. For deterministic replies we run temp 0-0.2 and top_p 0.7-0.9. Max_tokens is both cost and safety control. We also support stop sequences and function/tool calling for structured outputs.
02:18 Maya Ortiz: Is there server-side rate limiting? we need per-tenant quotas.
02:23 Liam Chen: yes, hosted supports per-account and per-token quotas + rate limiting. You can also set per-route limits in the Console.
02:31 Aisha Khan: latency targets — what's typical p95 for short completions?
02:36 Priya Singh: on hosted with our curated models p95 for sub-100 token responses is typically 180-350ms depending on region and load. We surface detailed latency breakdowns in Console. For guaranteed p95 you'd look at Dedicated with reserved GPUs.
02:50 Derek Sloan: what about cost math compared to OpenAI?
02:53 Liam Chen: cost varies — we publish model unit economics and Optimize can recommend quantization and batching to reduce per token cost. For many production workloads the hosted path is competitive, and dedicated reduces unit cost at commit levels. We'll share a cost worksheet.
03:06 Maya Ortiz: ok demo part please
03:10 Priya Singh: switching to my screen — here's the Redwood Console quick tour: Models catalog, routes, and a request playground. I'll show a streaming response example.
03:22 Priya Singh: (screen) sending a playground request with stream=true. Note how partial tokens arrive in the UI; on the client side we expose a streaming client lib for Node and Python. You can also parse tokens and show typing UI.
03:34 Liam Chen: quick note, the streaming connection supports backpressure — if client is slow we continue to buffer but we recommend using chunked reads.
03:40 Derek Sloan: do you support acks or offsets when resuming?
03:44 Priya Singh: we issue sequence offsets in the stream meta so a client can ack up to a last seen token and request resume from a clear boundary. That helps with dedupe logic on reconnect.
03:55 Maya Ortiz: retry policy for 5xx or timeouts — automatic client retry?
03:59 Priya Singh: typical pattern: exponential backoff for idempotent calls with same token; for non-idempotent you should present a retry dialog to user. Redwood SDKs expose retry helpers with sensible defaults.
04:11 Aisha Khan: security — KMS, encryption at rest, SOC2?
04:15 Liam Chen: Redwood is SOC 2 Type II, we support customer-managed KMS keys for Private and Dedicated; for hosted we offer envelope encryption with provider KMS and can integrate with partner KMS for enterprise customers. We'll send the SOC2 and security pack.
04:30 Derek Sloan: SSO and RBAC?
04:33 Liam Chen: Console supports SAML/SSO, SCIM provisioning, and fine-grained RBAC per-route. For API keys you can mint short-lived tokens.
04:41 Maya Ortiz: VPC peering or private link? We can't send PII outside our VPC in some regions.
04:47 Priya Singh: hosted can offer private network options in select regions (private endpoints / VPC peering). For stricter needs Dedicated or Private deployments are common. We also have audit logs and retention controls.
05:00 Derek Sloan: what about deployment toggles? say fallback to smaller model when load spikes?
05:05 Priya Singh: yes — routing policies can fallback to cheaper model variants or a lower tier region. Rollouts support canary and traffic splits. The runtime can also autoretry to a different pool if capacity is constrained.
05:18 Maya Ortiz: how do you measure quality regressions after model changes?
05:22 Liam Chen: Optimize ties evaluations to prompt sets — you can run periodic evals and attach alerts if metrics like agreement or hallucination rate degrade. We'll show benchmarking scripts in the repo.
05:33 Aisha Khan: demo question — show us a sample Node streaming client?
05:36 Priya Singh: sure, I pasted a snippet in the chat. It shows creating a stream, wiring the token handler, and providing an idempotency key. Note the snippet includes retry helpers. (transcription error: snippet -> snipet)
05:52 Maya Ortiz: in terms of uptime and SLA for hosted?
05:55 Liam Chen: hosted has SLOs; SLA-backed uptime is available on Dedicated contracts. We'll include SLO and SLA docs in the pack.
06:03 Derek Sloan: will you support model pinning? we want deterministic output for compliance reasons.
06:07 Priya Singh: you can pin model versions per route in Console; that ensures you don't drift across upstream model releases. We also support immutable model ids for audits.
06:16 Maya Ortiz: ok cost/latency tradeoff sounds clear. One more — how do you handle streaming + moderation or safety filters?
06:25 Priya Singh: safety filters can run concurrent to generation, you get a safety score in the metadata. For high-risk flows we recommend synchronous moderation pre-generation or post-run filtering with a hold state before committing to KV cache.
06:40 Liam Chen: quick recap — we covered streaming mechanics, idempotency and retries, params, Console demo and Optimize basics, and security.
06:49 Maya Ortiz: thanks — very helpful. We'll review and share QPS targets.
06:53 Derek Sloan: can you send example infra diagram for hosted vs dedicated connectivity?
06:56 Liam Chen: yes, Priya will attach that to the follow-up.
06:59 Aisha Khan: any gotchas we should test in POC?
07:02 Priya Singh: test reconnect + resume logic, run parallel sessions to validate KV cache behavior, and run batch benchmarks with the script we'll share. Also test SSO provisioning flow in Console.
07:14 Maya Ortiz: timeline: if POC looks good we'd aim for a fall launch, but early pilot next quarter.
07:20 Liam Chen: excellent — we'll send docs and a proposed POC plan.
07:25 Priya Singh: I'll follow up with recording and the benchmark repo link.
07:30 Liam Chen: Any final Qs?
07:33 Maya Ortiz: none, thanks everyone.
07:35 Liam Chen: thanks all — we'll follow up with next steps.
